newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China officials urge direct Taiwan trade links.
newsitem.headline: China officials urge direct Taiwan trade links.

text.p: Visiting Chinese economic officials urged rival Taiwan on Thursday to establish direct links with China, saying this would protect Taiwanese investment on the communist mainland.
On the second day of a 12-day trip regarded by government officials here as a propaganda visit, the group said China had completed a draft plan that would protect Taiwan businessmen.
But for the sides to enhance economic relations, Taiwan must allow direct trade, postal and transportation links with the mainland, the Chinese delegation said.

"Authorities will continue to follow the eight-point proposal by (China's President) Jiang (Zemin) to develop cross-strait trade and economic ties," said Liu Zhentao, economic bureau director of China's cabinet-level Taiwan Affairs Office.
He told reporters that Jiang's proposal remained the main guideline for Beijing in dealing with Taiwan following the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on February 19.
In a proposal made in January 1995, Jiang called for more trade and economic ties and offered a meeting between leaders of both sides, but warned against any independence move by Taiwan.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war ended in 1949, but Beijing still regards the island as a Chinese province subject to eventual re-unification.
Taiwan bans direct links with China, and all trade and investment activities must be routed through a third area, principally Hong Kong.

The 15-member delegation, invited by Taiwan's private Chinese National Federation of Industries, included some of the most senior mainland officials to have visited Taiwan in recent years, despite strained bilateral relations.
But Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council, which formulates Taiwan's China policies, brushed off the visit as propaganda.
"It appears to me that their visit is just another propaganda trip," a council official told Reuters by telephone.
Chinese official Wang Hui said Beijing had completed regulations it hoped could be implemented this year to protect the rights and interests of Taiwan investment projects in China.

"The State Council (cabinet) has completed a draft to strengthen protection for Taiwan businessmen on the mainland," said Wang, deputy chief of the Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao affairs department under China's Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Ministry.
About 30,000 Taiwanese have pumped an estimated US$30 billion into the mainland since the Nationalist government permitted indirect trade and investment with China in the late 1980s.
But for Taiwan and China to sign an investment protection agreement, both sides must have "direct links and reciprocal exchange", he said.
